title: Sound, good, weak
hookLine: hadith are graded: sahih, hasan, da'if, and fabricated

cards: After report upon report in his collection, al-Tirmidhi does something you can see right on the page. He steps out from behind the book and gives his own verdict.
Abu Isa said, he writes, using the name he went by: this hadith is hasan sahih. Or: this hadith is gharib, rare, and we know it only through this chain.
Like a teacher writing a note in the margin of the exam he hands you. The report, and then a grade. Today, sahih.

teach.b: Sahih means sound, healthy, whole. In the definition laid out by Ibn al-Salah, a sound hadith has a connected chain, every link meeting the next. Every narrator is upright in character and precise in memory.
And the report is free of two hidden problems: oddness, where it goes against what more reliable narrators report, and a concealed defect that only careful comparison reveals.
Next, hasan: good. Close to sound, but a narrator's precision is a step lighter: honest, not quite as sharp. Scholars of law still act on a good hadith.
Then da'if: weak. Something in the conditions is missing. A gap in the chain.
A narrator nobody can vouch for. A memory known to wander. Weak doesn't mean false.
It means not established. Scholars differ on whether, and how, a weak report may be used for encouragement, and this block comes back to that.
Below weak is mawdu': fabricated. That isn't a grade of the Prophet's words at all. It's a forgery, words put in his mouth, and scholars named it so it couldn't hide among the others.
Two more things. Grades can differ: one scholar may call a report good where another calls it weak, and both show their reasons.

And Shia hadith scholarship has its own grading terms, some with the same names, weighed by its own conditions. So a grade isn't a stamp from nowhere. It's a scholar's judgment, with the work showing.

how: Hadith scholars grade reports as sahih (sound), hasan (good) or da'if (weak), and identify fabricated ones; modern editions of the collections often print a scholar's grade beside each report, and Shia scholarship uses its own grading terms.

o: sound: an unbroken chain of upright, precise narrators
any report that sounds wise, whatever its chain
any report found in a well-known book of the Prophet's words

games.q: sound, good, weak — tap the pairs.
p: good: a step lighter in memory

s: weak means the scholars proved it false
weak means not established; fabricated is a separate, lower category.
al-Tirmidhi gives his own verdict after reports
"this hadith is hasan sahih", he writes, among other verdicts.
every scholar gives every hadith the same grade
grades can differ, and scholars show their reasons.

games.q: you're grading a report. every narrator is honest and sharp, but one of them never met the man he quotes. what grade?
games.why: a sound hadith needs a connected chain. a missing link makes it weak, not fabricated: honest people, a gap between them.

practice: Choose one saying of the Prophet you've heard more than once, from this path, a parent, a sermon or a poster, and say it to yourself. Do you know its grade, or which collection it's in?
If not, that's the gap to notice: think where you'd look, a teacher you trust, a printed collection, a reference that shows the grade beside the text, and if you pray, ask to carry only what's sound.

wordCard.voice: Sahih. Sound: an unbroken chain of upright, precise narrators, with no oddness and no hidden defect. Beside it, hasan, good, and da'if, weak. Today's word.

orig.note: sound, healthy, whole: the highest grade of a single report.

carryVoice: Your line: graded with care. Weak means not established; forged means not his at all. That's today.
